name: Cysteamine cream (Cyspera)

card.summary: A topical depigmenting cream used to fade melasma and other dark patches so skin tone looks more even.
card.note: Cysteamine has a strong odor in some formulations; the stabilized cream is described as milder.

quick.overview:
Cysteamine is a naturally occurring compound that is used in a topical cream, sold as Cyspera, to lighten dark patches such as melasma. Fading uneven pigment gives a more even, clear-looking complexion.

It is also used orally and as eye drops for cystinosis. For skin, randomized trials of cysteamine 5% cream in melasma, mostly from Iran, report greater pigment reduction than placebo and comparisons with hydroquinone-based treatments.
quick.how: The cream is applied to pigmented areas, typically in a daily routine over several months in the trials, along with sun protection. Products and regimens differ; clinical programs include office-based and home-based use.
quick.risks: Reported adverse events in studies were minor and transient, such as irritation. Older cysteamine formulations had a foul odor, and a stabilized 5% hydrochloride form was developed to be milder [1]. Oral cysteamine has a separate and wider set of side effects.

lead: Cysteamine is an organosulfur compound made in the body during coenzyme A breakdown. Oral and eye-drop forms treat cystinosis, and topical use may lighten skin darkened by melasma, sun exposure or post-inflammatory marks [6]. Cyspera is a branded 5% cream.

For appearance, it targets uneven pigmentation, giving skin a more uniform tone. A 2015 randomized trial of 50 patients with epidermal melasma compared 5% cysteamine with placebo over four months and found significantly greater pigment reduction on colorimetry in the cysteamine group [3].

A 2021 systematic review of eight studies concluded the cream appears comparably effective for melasma with minor, transient adverse events, but noted small samples [1]. A randomized trial in Victoria, Australia compared cysteamine with hydroquinone in 20 participants [4].

angle.text: People with melasma or marks use it to fade dark patches on the face. Results in trials are measured by melanin readings and severity scores over weeks to months.

paras: Used topically for melasma and other hyperpigmentation [6][1].
Oral capsules and eye drops treat cystinosis [6].

A placebo-controlled trial of 50 patients found significant differences in Mexameter differences at 2 and 4 months, with the cysteamine group dropping from 75.2 to 26.2 and placebo from 68.9 to 60.7 [3]. A systematic review of eight studies, mostly Iranian, found significant melanin and satisfaction improvements [1]. A randomized trial compared it with hydroquinone [4]. Other studies include a split-face microneedling radiofrequency trial [5] and a systematic review of hyperpigmentation formulations [2].
The review reports minor and transient adverse events [1]. Oral cysteamine can cause bad breath, body odor and gastrointestinal effects [6].
Randomized trials in melasma include [3], [4] and [5], plus a systematic review [1]. Authors note limited sample sizes [1].

timeline.event: Randomized placebo-controlled trial of cysteamine 5% in epidermal melasma published in the British Journal of Dermatology [3].
Systematic review of topical cysteamine for melasma [1].
